gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 running a 630 kWh/yr fridge uses about 1,966 Wh a day once you add the station's own 10 W idle draw (240 Wh a day). At that load, the 200 W solar bundle would need about 10.7 hours at full rated output every day to keep up. That is not possible, so the 2×200 W bundle (about 5.3 rated-output hours) is the smallest kit that can sustain the fridge on sun.
standout_why: I compared the cited basc.pnnl.gov page (630 kWh/yr example and surge guidance, with no solar recharge time or formula), the cited itechguides page (runtime = Wh ÷ W, maker UPS claims and the FridgePower's 4 W standby, but no calculation of the solar watts needed to keep up), stormwatts (kWh/yr to battery Wh/day at 0.85, with no idle draw, solar or refill time), usablekwh (says the solar ceiling 'turns a two-day outage into an indefinite one' but has no panel-vs-load arithmetic or idle draw) and powerstations.reviews (sends readers to another page for the sun-hours math). None of them checks the panel watts against the fridge's daily Wh plus the station's idle Wh, and that check decides between the 200 W and 2×200 W bundles from the same store.
kit_items: Power station: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 (2,073.6 Wh, 2,600 W). Storage Review measured 1.91 kWh delivered. That is about 23 h for a 630 kWh/yr fridge plus 10 W idle: 1,910 Wh ÷ 81.9 W. Its 1,000 W, 12–60 V, 20 A solar input has room for 400 W of panels.

Solar panels: 2× BLUETTI 200 W, sold as the store's Elite 200 V2 + 2×200 W bundle. Daily need is about 1,966 Wh AC, or about 2,140 Wh into the battery at the 92% Storage Review measured. 400 W supplies that in about 5.3 h at full rated output. 200 W would need about 10.7 h, so one panel cannot keep up.
Optional for larger fridges or cloudy regions: the Elite 200 V2 + 2×350 W bundle (700 W). 2,140 Wh ÷ 700 W ≈ 3.1 h at full rated output.

findings.label: Example refrigerator daily energy
findings.value: 630 kWh/yr ≈ 1.7 kWh/day; extreme summer heat can raise daily use by 20% or more
findings.source_title: Emergency Air Conditioning and Food Refrigeration | Building America Solution Center
findings.note: 630,000 Wh ÷ 365 = 1,726 Wh/day ≈ 71.9 W average. The page's own advice is to pick a fridge under 2 kWh/day.

findings.label: Example startup surge
findings.value: 3.5 A fridge ≈ 420 W running, ≈ 800 W to start; older or side-by-side units up to 2,000 W
findings.source_title: Emergency Air Conditioning and Food Refrigeration | Building America Solution Center
findings.note: 3.5 A × 120 V = 420 W. The Elite 200 V2's 2,600 W rated output is above the 2,000 W worst case BASC cites.

findings.label: Efficient fridge daily energy (StormWatts table)
findings.source_title: How Big a Power Station Do You Need to Run a Refrigerator During an Outage? | StormWatts
findings.note: Adding 240 Wh/day of station idle gives 1,336 Wh AC. ÷ 0.92 ≈ 1,452 Wh into the battery, which is ≈ 3.6 h at full rated output on 400 W of panels or ≈ 7.3 h on 200 W.

findings.label: Capacity, output, solar and AC input (maker's Canadian page)
findings.value: 2,073.6 Wh; 2,600 W rated; Power Lifting to 3,900 W (resistive only); PV 12–60 V, 20 A, 1,000 W max; AC input 1,800 W max

findings.label: Measured AC energy delivered and to recharge
findings.source_title: Portable Power Meets Lab-Grade Reliability: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review (Dylan Dougherty, StorageReview, 2025-04-25)
findings.note: 1,910 ÷ 2,073.6 = 92% of rated capacity delivered as AC; 1.91 ÷ 2.44 ≈ 78% round trip on AC charging. On-battery runtime for a 630 kWh/yr fridge plus 10 W idle: 1,910 Wh ÷ (71.9 + 10) W ≈ 23.3 h.

findings.label: Idle draw with AC and DC outputs on (maker spec as quoted by reviewer)
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 portable power station review (Greg Cleveland, The Gadgeteer)
findings.note: This is a quoted spec, not a measurement ('Low idle consumption, 10w/h with AC and DC left on'). 10 W × 24 h = 240 Wh/day. Added to 1,726 Wh that makes 1,966 Wh/day AC. ÷ 0.92 ≈ 2,137 Wh into the battery, which is ≈ 10.7 h at full rated output on 200 W, ≈ 5.3 h on 400 W and ≈ 3.1 h on 700 W.
